expected_evidence: Observatory logbook/register entries from beta-observatory documenting the sighting date, time, and use of transit-timing-method
Published announcement or circular (e.g., an IAU-style astronomical circular or comet bureau notice) crediting alpha-team with the comet-q sighting
Peer-reviewed or institutional bulletin/journal article by alpha-team describing the transit-timing measurements
Correspondence (letters/telegrams) between beta-observatory staff and other observatories confirming or disputing the sighting
Raw timing/transit data sheets or photographic/chart records from the transit instrument used
Institutional archive records (observatory annual reports, staff rosters) confirming alpha-team's presence and activity at beta-observatory during 1900-1999
response.rationale: The hypothesis places this event in the interval [1900,1999], i.e. the 20th-century/modern era, but the supplied detectability table only covers prehistoric-to-classical periods (upper-paleolithic through classical, none later than ~classical antiquity). None of the table rows are directly applicable to a modern astronomical observation, so I cannot simply look up a value - I am extrapolating (model-prior, unverified) that 20th-century scientific institutions have vastly higher documentary reliability than any period listed, since the classical row already reaches 0.85 for textual evidence using ancient inscriptions/manuscripts, and modern observatories additionally benefit from standardized international astronomical reporting (comet circulars, journals), photographic/instrumental records, and archival preservation practices essentially guaranteeing multiple redundant records. For a real 20th-century comet sighting by a named team at a named observatory using a specific timing method, we would expect it to appear in international comet-discovery/observation circulars, observatory annual reports, and possibly peer-reviewed astronomical literature - all of which are standardly archived and searchable in modern astronomical history databases. Given this, the near-total absence of any such record (no observatory log, no circular entry, no journal citation, no correspondence) is very hard to explain by low detectability, since detectability for this modern context should be high (~0.9-0.95 for textual/astronomical evidence), unlike the low or zero values seen in the paleolithic/holocene rows. Therefore an absence of evidence here weighs more heavily toward the hypothesis being false, fabricated, or misattributed (e.g., wrong actor, wrong observatory, wrong comet designation, or wrong method) rather than toward evidence having been lost to poor preservation. I flag this period mismatch explicitly: the detectability table as given does not natively support this hypothesis's stated interval, and my adjustment value is a model-prior extrapolation, not derived from the table itself.
